newsitem.title: GERMANY: Union targets job security as part of wage demand.
newsitem.headline: Union targets job security as part of wage demand.

text.p: Germany's largest metal workers union, the powerful IG Metall, Tuesday laid out its pay demand for 1997, putting a clear emphasis on job security as a major goal of the pay negotiations.
The union's chairman Klaus Zwickel said after a meeting of IG Metall's management board that union leaders plan to seek wage increases of 4.5 percent to 5 percent for next year.

That range was immediately rejected by metal employers group Gesamtmetall, who said it would at most be willing to discuss a wage increase in line with inflation, currently at around 1.5 percent in Germany.
But IG Metall's Zwickel made it clear that as much as half of the overall pay claim could be effected through measures aimed at securing jobs rather than direct wage increases.

"We have been put under pressure by dramatic erroneous developments in employment policies," Zwickel told a news conference. "Job security will have the highest priority for IG Metall in the 1997 wage round."
The total wage demand is made up of two components, a 2.5 percent to 3 percent compensation for increased productivity and two percent for expected inflation.

"The productivity component of 2-1/2 to three percent, should be used exclusively for goals related to job security policies," Zwickel said, adding that the union's aim in terms of basic pay would be to at least keep up with inflation.
Gesamtmetall Chairman Werner Stumpfe appeared to accept the principle that real wages should not fall, but repeated earlier insistences that overall labour costs needed to be cut.
"Wage increases in line with inflation could be discussed -- but only if savings in contractual labour costs also follow," he said in a statement.
Economists focused on Zwickel's emphasis on job security measures as potentially paving the way for a final agreement that might include a relatively modest wage increase.
"The industry is in the midst of structural changes that tend to dampen wage demands," said Timo Klein, senior German economist at analysis group MMS International.
Klein added that this could lead to a settlement involving a wage increase of 2 percent to 2.5 percent.
